en: Start with the Map: Qinling, the Wei, and the Wall
zh: 先看西安地图：秦岭、渭河与城墙
ja: まず西安の地図を読む：秦嶺・渭河・城壁

p.src: When you open a map of Xi'an, do not begin with the Bell Tower. Zoom out beyond the wall. The Qinling range lies to the south and the Wei River crosses the plain to the north; the Bell Tower, the pagodas and several palace sites sit between them. Once that frame is clear, the sequence of capitals and their sites is easier to follow. Chang'an is not simply an old name for the Xi'an enclosed by today's wall. Successive capitals chose different sites in response to mountains, rivers, loess terraces and roads, so their footprints do not fully coincide.

caption.zh: 从南侧走近永宁门，先看城墙怎样横向切开视野，再找城门、墙顶和背后的现代楼群。这里适合建立‘明城墙只围住今日老城核心’的第一印象。
caption.ja: 南側から永寧門へ近づくときは、城壁が視界を横切る長さをまず見て、門、壁上、背後の現代建築を重ねて捉える。明代城壁が囲むのは現在の旧城中心部だという感覚を、ここでつかめる。
caption.en: Approaching Yongning Gate from the south, first take in how the wall cuts across the view, then locate the gate, wall top and modern buildings beyond. It is a useful first measure of the compact core enclosed by the Ming wall.

p.src: North of the Qinling, the land does not descend in one even slope. Mountains give way to dissected hills, loess tablelands and piedmont fans, then to the plain of the Wei and its tributaries. Buildings and roads hide much of this relief, but place names such as Longshouyuan, Bailuyuan and Shaolingyuan still identify raised, comparatively level ground. From the edge of a tableland or the higher ground of a palace site, the relationship among sightlines, watercourses and city sites becomes easier to read.

p.src: This map makes one point: today's wall occupies a small area between the Qinling and the Wei River system. Solid lines come from open geographic data; dashed reaches indicate river sections missing from the public centreline data. This is an orientation diagram, not a navigation map or a guide to the exact riverbank.

caption.en: Xi'an lies between the Qinling foothills and the Wei River system. Today's wall is shown in vermilion; dashed reaches generalise incomplete centreline data.

p.src: Guanzhong is often described as a region enclosed by four passes. Historical sources, however, use different boundaries and different sets of passes: some name two, some four, and some imply a wider area. A traveller does not need to force it into a fixed outline. It is more useful to see the Wei River plain as its core, with mountain gateways narrowing the main routes in and out. The setting favoured farming, water supply and defence, but it did not remove the cost of moving grain, people and orders over long distances.

p.src: The traditional Eight Waters are the Wei, Jing, Feng, Lao, Jue, Hao, Chan and Ba. They are not eight evenly spaced moats around the present wall. Some join north of the city, some descend from the Qinling's northern slopes, and others are connected with Western Zhou Fenghao, Han and Tang waterworks, or routes to the east. The phrase 'Eight Waters around Chang'an' summarizes the waterways around the capitals; it does not describe a precise ring. On a map, check which river, loess tableland and mountain valley lie near a site. That is more useful than memorizing eight names.

p.src: These rivers do not belong only to antiquity. The 2025 approval for Xi'an's territorial plan calls for restoration of both the Qinling ecological barrier and the Wei River basin. Municipal environmental material also identifies the Qinling mountains as a water-conservation area. Rivers on historical maps therefore help explain the present city as well: they account for the location of settlements and sites, and show why valleys, riverbanks and archaeological parks are affected by season, protection boundaries and city management.

p.src: To find your bearings in Xi'an, remember three references: the Qinling to the south, the Wei to the north, and the Ming-derived wall enclosing a small historic district between them. In clear weather, use the southern mountains to check direction. When the mountains are not visible, establish whether you are near the wall, the pagodas, Xi'an North station or the Lintong side of the city. Do not treat 'inside the wall' as all of Chang'an. The outer-city enclosures of Sui Daxing and Tang Chang'an extended far beyond today's wall, and many important sites remain in separate parts of modern Xi'an.

p.src: The next chapter therefore asks not 'how many dynasties?' but where each capital placed its palaces, markets, roads and water system. Fenghao, Han Chang'an, Sui Daxing and Tang Chang'an, and Ming-Qing Xi'an do not fully overlap. Keep the terrain relationships from this chapter in mind: the layered capital map can then show how the city sites moved, without suggesting that all of them lay inside today's wall.
